title: Fitting and Clustering of Longitudinal Data Using CONNECTOR
author: Simone Pernice
materials: The number of clusters - G CONNECTOR provides two different plots to properly guide to set the number of clusters. Two measures of proximity are introduced: the total tightness (T) and the functional Davied-Bouldin index (fDB): as the number of clusters increases, the total tightness decreases to zero, the value which is attained when the number of fitted clusters is equal to the number of sampled curves; the functional David Bouldin (fDB) index: it is a cluster separation measure. A proper number of clusters can be inferred as large enough to let the total tightness drop down to little values over which it does not decrease substantially. Hence, we look for the location of an elbow the plot of the total tightness against the number of clusters. Furthermore, the optimal choice of clusters, then, will be that which minimizes this average blend. Let us note that the random initialization of the k-means algorithm to get initial cluster memberships into the FCM algorithm and the stochasticity characterizing the method lead to some variability among different runs. For these reasons, multiple runs are necessary to identify the most frequent clustering fixed a number of clusters ( G ). To effectively take advantage of those two measures, CONNECTOR supplies the function ClusterAnalysis which repeats the clustering procedure a number of times equal to the parameter runs and for each of the number of clusters given in the parameter G . ClusteringList G = 2:5, p = p, runs = 100) The output of the function is a list of three objects (i) $Clusters.List : the list of all the clustering divisions obtained varying among the input G values, (ii) $seed : the seed sets before running the method, (iii) $runs : the number of runs. Specifically, the object storing the clustering obtained with G = 2 (i.e., ClusteringList$Clusters.List$G2 ) is a list of three elements: $ClusterAll : the list of all the possible FCM parameters values that can be obtained through each run. In details, the item $ParamConfig.Freq reports the number of times that the respectively parameters configuration (stored in $FCM ) is found. Let us note, that the sum might be not equal to the number of runs since errors may occur; $ErrorConfigurationFit : list of errors that could be obtained by running the FCM method with extreme parameters configurations; $h.selected : the dimension of the mean space, denoted as h , selected to perform the analysis. In details, this parameter gives a further parametrization of the mean curves allowing a lower-dimensional representation of the curves with means in a restricted subspace. Its value is choose such that the inequality h ≤ min ( G −1, p ) holds. Better clusterings are obtained with higher values of h , but this may lead to many failing runs. In this cases h values is decreased until the number of successful runs are higher than a specific constraint which can be defined by the user (by default is 100% of successful runs). # the output structure str(ClusteringList, max.level = 2, vec.len=1) ## List of 4 ## $ Clusters.List:List of 4 ## ..$ G2:List of 2 ## ..$ G3:List of 2 ## ..$ G4:List of 2 ## ..$ G5:List of 2 ## $ CONNECTORList:List of 6 ## ..$ Dataset :'data.frame': 241 obs. of 3 variables: ## ..$ LenCurv : num [1:21] 9 9 ... ## ..$ LabCurv :'data.frame': 21 obs. of 5 variables: ## ..$ TimeGrid : num [1:50] 3 5 ... ## ..$ ColFeature : chr [1:5] "#FF0000" ... ## ..$ PlotTimeSeries_plot:List of 9 ## .. ..- attr(*, "class")= chr [1:2] "gg" ... ## $ seed : num 2404 ## $ runs : num 100 str(ClusteringList$Clusters.List$G2, max.level = 3, vec.len=1) ## List of 2 ## $ ClusterAll:List of 2 ## ..$ :List of 2 ## .. ..$ FCM :List of 4 ## .. ..$ ParamConfig.Freq: int 43 ## ..$ :List of 2 ## .. ..$ FCM :List of 4 ## .. ..$ ParamConfig.Freq: int 57 ## $ h.selected: num 1 ClusteringList The function IndexesPlot.Extrapolation generated two plots reported in Figure 6. In details, the tightness and fDB indexes are plotted for each value of G . Each value of G is associated with a violin plot created by the distribution of the index values collected from the runs performed. The blue line shows the most probable configuration which will be exploited hereafter. IndexesPlot.Extrapolation(ClusteringList)-> indexes indexes$Plot Fig. 6 Violin Plots of the total tightness (T) calculated on each run and for different number of clusters G (right panel). Violin Plots of the fDB calculated on each run and for different number of clusters G (left panel) G = 4 corresponds to the optimal choice for our example, since it represents the elbow for the tightness indexes (right panel) and explicitly minimizes the fDB indexes (left panel).The variability of the two measures among runs, exhibited in Figure 6 , is related to the random initialization of the k-means algorithm to get initial cluster memberships from points. The stability of the clustering procedure can be visualized through the stability matrix extrapolated by the function ConsMatrix.Extrapolation , as shown in Figure 7. The plot informs about the stability of the final clustering across different runs. Indeed, each cell of the matrix is coloured proportionally to the frequency of the two corresponding curves belonging to the same cluster across different runs. Hence the larger the frequencies are (which corresponds to warmer colours of the cells in the plot), the more stable is the final clustering. For each cluster the average stability value is reported. steps.title: Install CONNECTOR package
steps.instruction: In an R session load devtools (library(devtools)) and run install_github("https://github.com/qBioTurin/connector", ref="master") to install the CONNECTOR package.

steps.title: Set up optional Docker
steps.instruction: If Docker is preferred, install Docker per the official docs, ensure the user can run Docker without sudo (sudo groupadd docker; sudo usermod -aG docker $USER; log out and back in). Pull the CONNECTOR image with docker pull qbioturin/connector:latest and start the RStudio container: docker run --cidfile=dockerID -e DISABLE_AUTH=true -p 8787:8787 -d qbioturin/connector:latest, then open http://localhost:8787/. Alternatively, use CONNECTOR functions downloadContainers() and docker.run() to obtain and launch the image.

steps.title: Prepare input files
steps.instruction: Create two files: (1) an Excel file (GrowthDataFile) where each sample has a column named with its ID and a column named "time" containing the observation times; (2) a CSV (or txt) annotation file (AnnotationFile) whose first column is IDSample matching the IDs in the Excel file and subsequent columns contain sample features (e.g., Progeny). Ensure each sample has a unique ID and that the Excel file contains 48 columns for the 21 tumor‑growth curves.

steps.title: Import data into R
steps.instruction: Obtain the full path names of the example files (TimeSeriesFile and AnnotationFile) and call CONNECTORList <- DataImport(TimeSeriesFile, AnnotationFile). The function returns a list with four objects: Dataset (data frame with columns ID, Observation, Time), LenCurv (vector of curve lengths), LabCurv (data frame with IDSample, Progeny, Source, Real.Progeny, ID), and TimeGrid (numeric vector of time points). The summary will show Number of curves: 21; Min curve length: 7; Max curve length: 18.

steps.title: Optional data truncation
steps.instruction: If observations after 70 days should be removed, run trCONNECTORList <- DataTruncation(CONNECTORList, feature="Progeny", truncTime=70, labels=c("Time","Volume","Tumor Growth")). The function returns a list of truncated objects and prints a summary: Number of curves: 21; Min curve length: 7; Max curve length: 16; Number of truncated curves: 6; Min points deleted: 2; Max points deleted: 6. The plot stored in trCONNECTORList$PlotTimeSeries_plot shows a vertical black line at the truncation time.

steps.title: Select spline basis dimension p
steps.instruction: Use BasisDimension.Choice to explore p values in a user‑defined interval [p_min, p_max]. The function performs ten‑fold cross‑validation: data are split into 10 equal parts, the model is fitted on 9 parts and the log‑likelihood is computed on the held‑out part. Two plots are returned: CrossLogLikePlot (mean log‑likelihood vs. p) and KnotsPlot (sample curves with knot locations). Choose the smallest p that yields the largest mean cross‑validated log‑likelihood; in the example the optimal p is 3.

steps.title: Choose number of clusters G
steps.instruction: Define the number of clusters G according to the study needs (the protocol mentions G as a free parameter but does not prescribe a specific method; the user sets G before clustering).

steps.title: Run clustering and plot mean curves
steps.instruction: Execute ClusterWithMeanCurve(CONNECTORList, p=chosen_p, G=chosen_G) to fit the spline basis of dimension p and cluster the curves into G groups. The function plots sampled curves coloured by cluster together with the mean curve of each cluster and prints the following indexes for each cluster: S_k1 (total standard deviation), M_k1,k2 (distance between mean curves of clusters k1 and k2), R_k1 (cluster quality measure), and fDB (cluster validity index) together with their first and second derivatives (e.g., S, S_1, S_2). Example values are shown for clusters A, B, and C in the original text.

steps.title: List samples per cluster
steps.instruction: Call NumberSamples <- CountingSamples(feature="Progeny") to obtain a data frame listing, for each cluster, the number of samples and their IDs. The returned object contains two data frames: $Counting (columns Cluster, Progeny, n) and $ClusterNames (columns ID, Cluster).

steps.title: Generate discriminant plots
steps.instruction: Use DiscriminantPlot(FCMplots, h=1) to plot the first functional linear discriminant α₁ versus its variability, or DiscriminantPlot(FCMplots, h=2) to plot α₁ versus α₂. For h>2 the function performs a PCA to obtain additional components, which are plotted with explained variance in brackets. In the case study, h=2 produces a plot coloured by cluster membership (Figure 9) and another coloured by the "Progeny" feature (Figure 10).

steps.title: Identify high‑discrimination time points
steps.instruction: Retrieve the discriminant functions with MaxDiscrPlots <- DiscriminantFunction(FCMplots). The resulting plots (MaxDiscrPlots[[1]]) display the discriminant curves; time points with large absolute values (positive or negative) correspond to the most discriminatory measurements (e.g., early and late measurements).

steps.title: Plot estimated individual curves
steps.instruction: Create spline plots of the fitted and predicted curves with confidence intervals by running PlotSpline <- Spline.plots(FCMplots). Access the individual plot objects (e.g., PlotSpline$`*1*`) to view each sample’s observed points (blue), estimated spline (red), cluster mean curve (black), and the grey confidence‑interval band (as shown for sample ID = 1 in Figure 12).

steps.title: Visualize raw curves and time grid
steps.instruction: Generate a coloured line plot of the sampled curves with PlotTimeSeries(CONNECTORList, feature="Progeny") (Figure 1). Use DataVisualization(CONNECTORList) to produce a heat‑map of the time‑grid density (Figure 2). The heat‑map shows each pair of time points (x, y) coloured by the number of samples that have observations at both times, guiding decisions such as the truncation at 70 days.
